title: HP's Printer Is the Bait
summary: HP sold $5.8 billion of printers last year and $10.9 billion of ink and toner. Its own annual report explains why cartridges are where the money is.
tags: why is printer ink so expensive

hooks.hook: HP sold $5.8 billion of printers last year. It sold almost twice that in ink and toner.
HP's own annual report calls its cartridges high margin.
The cheapest printer is the most expensive one you'll ever own.

sources: HP Inc. fiscal 2025 results (year ended Oct 31, 2025), Exhibit 99.1: total net revenue $55,295M; Personal Systems revenue $38,532M, earnings from operations $2,054M (5.3%); Printing revenue $16,702M, earnings from operations $3,118M (18.7%); Supplies $10,916M (2024: $11,295M); Commercial Printing $4,633M; Consumer Printing $1,153M: https://www.hp.com/us-en/newsroom/press-releases/2025/hp-inc-reports-fiscal-2025-full-year-and-fourth-quarter-results.html

HP Inc. fiscal 2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A: "While our big tank printers typically have a higher initial margin than our traditional in cartridge printers, they do not result in follow-on sales of high margin traditional ink cartridges and, as a result, may have lower overall device lifetime profitability." Commercial and Consumer Printing exclude supplies: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/47217/000004721725000071/hpq-20251031.htm
Our calculations: printer hardware $4,633M + $1,153M = $5,786M; supplies / printing revenue = 65%; supplies change -3.4%.

scenes.narration: Last year, HP sold {$5.8 billion|five point eight billion dollars} worth of printers. It sold almost twice that in ink and toner.
Printers: {$5.8 billion.|five point eight billion.} Ink and toner: {$10.9 billion.|ten point nine billion.}

scenes.narration: The printer isn't really the product. It's the bait. And HP's own annual report tells you why.
Part one. The bait and the hook.
It's an old trick called razor and blades. Sell the machine cheap. Then sell the refills, again and again, for years.
Home printers, the ones most of us buy, brought HP just {$1.2 billion.|one point two billion dollars.} A small slice next to the ink.
At HP, ink and toner made up about {65 percent|sixty-five percent} of all printing revenue last year.
For every dollar spent on an HP printer last year, about a dollar ninety went on HP ink and toner.

Now compare it with HP's computers. Computers brought in {$38.5 billion|thirty-eight point five billion} and earned {$2.1 billion.|two point one billion.} Printing brought in less than half that, and earned {$3.1 billion.|three point one billion.}
HP sells far more computers. It makes more money from printing.
If you like seeing the receipts behind everyday prices, subscribe. New ones every Tuesday and Friday.
Part two. HP's own receipt.
Some printers now come with big ink tanks you refill yourself from a bottle. Here's how HP's annual report describes them.
They do not result in follow-on sales of high margin traditional ink cartridges.

data.quote: They do not result in follow-on sales of *high margin* traditional ink cartridges.
data.note: on its big refillable tank printers

scenes.narration: In plain words: the cartridges are where the money is. A printer you refill yourself breaks the hook.
That's why tank printers cost more up front. HP says they carry a higher margin at the start, because there's less to earn later.
And the switch shows. HP's ink and toner sales fell about {3 percent|three percent} last year.

data.label: HP ink and toner sales, fiscal 2025

scenes.narration: HP's report lists other threats too: cheaper cartridges from other brands, and people simply printing less, because more of life is digital.
Part three. The real price.
So when a printer looks cheap, don't look at the box. Look at what a year of ink costs. That's the real price.
Three questions before you buy. What does a cartridge cost? How many pages does it print? And does a refillable tank model cost less over a year?
The cheapest printer can be the most expensive one you ever own. Next time: are Black Friday deals even real?
